source.title: xLSTM Scaling Laws: Competitive Performance with Linear Time-Complexity
source.authors: Maximilian Beck; Kajetan Schweighofer; Sebastian Bock; Sebastian Lehner; S. Hochreiter

record.file_problem: none; full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It applies parametric loss-surface fitting and IsoFLOP sweeps to validation cross-entropy and compute-optimal model/token counts, using methods closely aligned with the original scaling-law studies, on Transformer and xLSTM runs.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own validation-loss scaling fits, over-training exponents, Pareto comparison, and compute-optimal parameter/token fits. The paper does not validate small-run forecasts against much larger held-out runs. It states that downstream tasks and different training-data distributions are outside its scope. Inference runtime results do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Uses Chinchilla's IsoFLOP and parametric loss-surface methods on held-out validation cross-entropy (80M–7B params, 2B–2T tokens, ~5 orders of compute). It fits loss power laws, compute-optimal N*(H) and D*(H), and fit sensitivity, for Transformer and xLSTM. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that xLSTM Pareto-dominates Transformers in loss vs compute and keeps constant power-law exponents when over-trained. Compute-optimal xLSTMs are larger, are trained on a similar number of tokens, and keep a stable size across context lengths, while Transformer optima shrink with context. A shared performance-vs-size relation holds for both architectures, and xLSTM is faster at inference. They note their parameter/token exponents (0.575/0.424) differ from Chinchilla's and, following Porian et al., attribute this to the learning-rate schedule. They also say their Transformer exponent reproduces Porian's.
record.recipe_differences: Uses IsoFLOP and parametric loss-surface approaches similar to prior scaling-law work, but applies them to xLSTM and Transformer runs with a more detailed architecture-specific FLOP calculation; γ is fitted freely and their training schedule and data are specific to this study.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted loss-surface parameters vary with Huber δ for values below 0.1; fitting γ freely improves fit quality. Batch size affects IsoFLOP loss profiles, while the reported 1e+20 FLOP comparison gives a similar optimal parameter count. Context length changes compute-optimal sizes, particularly for Transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: xLSTM Pareto-dominates Transformer in validation loss vs training FLOPs across ~5 orders of compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture choice (linear-time recurrent vs attention) shifts the loss–compute frontier at fixed scaling-law form.

record.problems: The fits and comparisons are limited to the paper's architectures, training recipe, and DCLM-BASELINE data. The study does not validate small-run extrapolations on much larger held-out runs, and reports no uncertainty intervals for its own fitted exponents. It does not test downstream tasks or other data distributions.

untested.parts: No held-out validation of small-run fits on much larger runs. The Table 23 projections to 175B are unvalidated extrapolations.
Budgets above 6e20 FLOPs; for context-specific fits, budgets above 3e19.
No controlled depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Downstream tasks explicitly out of scope.
Untested: whether curves bend away from a single power law at larger scale, effects of the data distribution, and parameter-counting conventions.

missing.what: Transformer a=0.575 falls inside Porian et al.'s CI (0.56, 0.59). The authors attribute the difference from Chinchilla (a=0.49, b=0.51) to the LR decay schedule, citing Porian.
Implied compute-optimal token/param ratio falls with size, e.g. Transformer 41.7 at 100M to 5.9 at 175B (xLSTM 28.3 to 4.8), versus a constant ~22 in Chinchilla. Values beyond 7B are extrapolated.
Compute-optimal N* and D* fitted as power laws of context length. Transformer N* exponent is about -0.15; xLSTM is about -0.03 to -0.04.
Varying batch size with model size produced loss offsets in IsoFLOP profiles, which is why the authors fixed batch size per budget.

record.verdict_notes: I changed the V3 'challenges' label to 'limits_scope': the unequal split comes from a known schedule effect that the authors themselves flag, which fits V7, not an absence of V3's stable-power relation. No uncertainty is reported on the paper's own exponents. The inference-runtime results bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: The fits cover the paper's tested architectures, data, and training setup; they do not establish the law for other data distributions or regimes.
No held-out test of power laws fitted only on small runs against runs orders of magnitude larger.
Tests fitted compute-optimal parameter and token scaling for the architectures and context lengths studied, not all model classes or compute budgets.
No controlled comparison isolating depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer experiments.
The paper explicitly does not investigate downstream tasks.
The study reports sensitivity to fitting and training choices, but does not test every listed source of disagreement or establish that curves bend away from power laws at larger scales.
